answers.title: Is it a defect, or is it normal?
answers.subtitle: The four questions people bring here most often, each with the test that answers it.

items.title: A dot that won't go away
items.summary: Dark on every color, white included, is a dead pixel and will not come back. One held color is stuck, and stuck pixels sometimes recover.
body: Step through solid colors and watch the dot. If it stays dark on every color, white included, it is a dead pixel and it will not come back. If it holds one color, or glows on black, it is stuck, and stuck pixels sometimes recover: the last frame of the Dead Pixel Test flashes colors over the spot for that purpose. Wipe the screen before you decide, because dust looks identical until it moves.

Whether it is worth a return depends less on the dot than on the calendar. Manufacturers allow a small number of faults per panel, count bright pixels more strictly than dark ones, and often replace a cluster while refusing scattered dots. A full row or column is a connection fault and almost always qualifies. Inside the retailer's return window none of those counts apply to you, which is the reason to test on the first day.

items.title: Glow on a black screen
items.summary: A glow that shifts and fades as you move is IPS glow, a trait of the panel type. Streaks along an edge that stay put are backlight bleed.
body: Nearly every LCD shows some light on black, because it makes black by blocking a backlight that never switches off. Put up a black screen in a dark room and lean about a foot to each side. A glow that shifts and fades as you move is IPS glow: a trait of the panel type, not a defect, and almost never covered by warranty. Streaks or patches along an edge that stay exactly where they are is backlight bleed.

A workable rule: if you can't see it while watching a film with the lights on, ignore it. A bright streak that shows during normal use, in dark game scenes or the bars around a film, is worth acting on. Judge it with your eyes at the brightness you actually use. Phone cameras take long exposures in the dark and make a faint haze look alarming. An OLED should show neither.

items.title: A ghost image on an OLED
items.summary: Play varied full-screen video for an hour or two, then look again. Image retention fades. Burn-in is exactly where you left it.
body: A faint outline of a taskbar, a channel logo or a game's HUD on a grey screen is one of two things, and time tells them apart. Play varied full-screen video for an hour or two, then look at the same grey field again. Image retention will have faded or gone. Burn-in will be exactly where you left it, because the pixels there are worn rather than stuck.

Look for a shape you recognize. Random blotches with no clear edge are more likely ordinary panel non-uniformity. Burn-in can't be removed, only slowed: lower the brightness, hide static elements, and let the panel run its compensation cycle. Some manufacturers now cover it under warranty for a limited period, so read that clause before assuming either way.

items.title: A fast monitor that doesn't feel fast
items.summary: A 144 Hz monitor reading 60 Hz is almost never faulty. The rate is not selected, the cable can't carry it, or a power-saving mode lowered it.
body: Measure it before you blame the panel. A 144 Hz monitor reading 60 Hz is almost never faulty: the higher rate hasn't been selected in the display settings, the cable or port can't carry it at that resolution, or a power-saving mode has lowered it. A reading within about 1 Hz of the rating is normal, since many displays run a fraction off their nominal rate.

If the number is right and motion still looks wrong, look at the trail behind a moving object. A smeared trail is ghosting from slow pixel response; a bright fringe is overshoot from overdrive set too high, and one notch down usually cures it. A soft, even blur with no afterimage is not a fault. Every display that holds each frame still produces it.

newer.title: Tests for newer screens
newer.subtitle: HDR, Mini-LED, OLED and high-refresh panels fail in ways a solid color can't show.

items.name: HDR Test
items.body: A real HDR image with brightness steps up to 1,600 nits, so you can see where your screen stops getting brighter.

items.name: PWM Flicker Test
items.body: Catch a flickering backlight with the pencil test, or a fast line that splits into copies on PWM-dimmed screens.

items.name: Wide Color Gamut (P3) Test
items.body: Logos hidden in Display P3 colors only appear if both your screen and your browser go beyond sRGB.

items.name: Frame Skipping Test
items.body: One cell lights per frame. Photograph it to find out whether an overclocked monitor quietly drops frames.

items.name: Blooming zone sweeps
items.body: Count how often the halo jumps as a square crosses the screen to estimate a Mini-LED's dimming zones.

items.name: Panning grey
items.body: Drifting grey bands that expose the dirty screen effect large TVs show when the camera pans.

prep.title: Before you test
prep.subtitle: A minute of setup makes every result easier to trust.

items.title: Let it warm up
items.body: A cold panel's brightness and color drift slightly at first. Give it about five minutes before testing, and 20–30 minutes before calibrating.

items.title: Switch off the filters
items.body: Night Light, Night Shift, True Tone, dynamic contrast and eye-care modes all change what you see. Turn them off for color and greyscale checks.

items.title: Dim the lights
items.body: Bleed, blooming and black-level tests need a properly dark room. Everything else works best dimly lit, with no reflections on the glass.

items.title: Use the native resolution
items.body: A scaled resolution softens fine detail and can blur a single bad pixel into its neighbors. Set your system to the panel's native resolution.

items.title: Fill the whole screen
items.body: Browser bars and the taskbar cover the edges, which is where bleed and dead pixels like to hide. Every test has a full-screen Start button.

items.title: Photograph what you find
items.body: Lock your phone camera's exposure, shoot in a dark room and note the date. That photo is your evidence for a return or warranty claim.

items.a: Yes. Every test is free to use, with no account and nothing to download. The site is supported by ads and donations.

items.q: Is anything uploaded when I run a test?
items.a: No. Your browser draws the test patterns on your own device, and nothing about your screen is sent anywhere. Like most websites, the site uses analytics and ads; the Privacy page lists what they collect.

items.q: Do the tests work on phones and tablets?
items.a: Yes, in any modern mobile browser. iPhone Safari doesn't let websites go truly full-screen, so there a test fills the browser window instead. The Touch Screen Test is built specifically for phones and tablets.

items.q: Can a browser test be accurate?
items.a: For defects you can see, yes: a full-screen solid color shows a dead pixel or backlight bleed just as clearly as dedicated software would. Measurements such as Delta E, brightness in nits or contrast ratio need a colorimeter; these tests show what those problems look like, not the numbers.

items.q: How many dead pixels are acceptable?
items.a: It depends on the manufacturer's pixel policy. One dark pixel often falls within the allowance, while bright pixels and clusters are treated more strictly. Inside the retailer's return window you usually don't need to argue about counts at all.

items.q: Which test should I run first on a new screen?
items.a: The Dead Pixel Test. Then check for bleed on black, uniformity on grey and banding in the gradients, and on a monitor or TV finish with the refresh rate. The new-device checklist in our guides walks through the full order.
